question: Can gradient-covariance active-subspace analysis be defined directly for real-valued functionals on a Hilbert space, estimated without first fixing a discretization, and used to improve visualization, regression, and optimization over function-valued inputs?

key_findings.claim: The paper defines a function-space analogue of the active-subspace matrix as an expectation of rank-one gradient operators.
key_findings.evidence: For a Frechet-differentiable functional f on a separable real Hilbert space H, the Riesz-represented gradient gives C = E[gradient f(U) tensor gradient f(U)]. Under a finite second-moment condition, C is trace class, compact, self-adjoint, and positive semidefinite, so its eigenfunctions form ordered directions whose eigenvalues equal average squared directional derivatives.

key_findings.claim: Working in the Hilbert space is not merely a notation for applying a finite-dimensional method after discretization.
key_findings.evidence: The authors exhibit a parameterized three-function example where active-subspace analysis in coefficient space identifies one dimension while direct functional analysis identifies the two-dimensional span of two basis functions. They also argue that functional eigenfunctions remain interpretable across mesh changes, whereas discretized eigenvectors can change meaning with the parameterization.

anchors.section: Section 2.2, parameterization example and practical consequences

key_findings.claim: Vanishing trailing spectrum implies exact ridge structure, while nonzero tails control a conditional-expectation surrogate's mean-squared error under an additional distributional assumption.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 states that if all eigenvalues after n vanish, gradients lie in the leading span, equal active projections imply equal function values and gradients, and f factors through the active projection. Theorem 2 bounds the mean-squared error of F(y)=E[f(U) given the active projection y] by a constant times the sum of trailing eigenvalues; that quantitative bound is conditional on Assumption 1 rather than universal over input laws.

key_findings.claim: A finite-rank empirical covariance operator permits an infinite-dimensional eigenanalysis through a B-by-B Gram matrix and is proved consistent.
key_findings.evidence: With B sampled functional gradients, the estimator is their average tensor product. Its nonzero eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are recovered from the finite Gram matrix G*G, with eigenfunctions expressed as linear combinations of sampled gradients. The authors prove almost-sure operator-norm consistency, convergence of isolated simple eigenfunctions, an expected O(B^-1/2) rate under a fourth-moment condition, and a Hilbert-Schmidt central limit theorem under a further appendix assumption.

key_findings.claim: On three PDE or mechanics functionals, projections onto learned functional active directions improve the tested downstream regression and optimization procedures over their chosen baselines.
key_findings.evidence: For Poisson control, laminar-jet reconstruction, and kirigami energy, the paper visualizes spectra and leading eigenfunctions. Leave-one-out KNN has lower error at its best K when distance is computed in the active projection rather than L2; for Poisson and kirigami, even the worst tested active K beats the best L2 K. In 100 Bayesian-optimization repetitions with 10 initial and 40 sequential evaluations, a search span built from empirical active eigenfunctions progresses faster than a span of random sampled functions on all three tasks.

method.core_idea: Lift the finite-dimensional gradient second-moment matrix to a compact covariance operator on a Hilbert space, then use its leading eigenfunctions as discretization-independent coordinates for function-valued inputs.
method.mechanism: Sample input functions from a chosen law, compute each functional gradient with a differentiable PDE or mechanics solver, and form the empirical average of rank-one gradient operators. Instead of materializing an infinite operator, diagonalize the finite Gram matrix of sampled gradients and reconstruct eigenfunctions as their weighted combinations. Project functions onto selected leading eigenfunctions for visualization and KNN distance, or use those eigenfunctions as the finite search basis for Bayesian optimization.
assumptions: The input domain is an open subset of a real separable Hilbert space and the target functional has an appropriate Frechet gradient.
The squared gradient norm is integrable; the rate result additionally needs a fourth moment, and the CLT and surrogate error bound use further stated assumptions.
The analyst's sampling law is representative of the portion of function space where sensitivity, prediction, or optimization matters.
A meaningful spectral gap exists when individual leading eigenfunctions, rather than only their joint invariant subspace, are interpreted.
Functional gradients and Hilbert inner products can be computed accurately enough under the numerical discretization.
The number of active directions is selected from spectral decay or retained energy without a task-independent guarantee.

techniques.role: Defines functional sensitivity through the expected tensor product of Riesz-represented gradients.
Compresses function-valued inputs into coordinates along leading average-sensitivity directions.
Recovers the empirical operator's nonzero eigensystem from a finite B-by-B matrix.
Defines the L2-optimal predictor based only on active coordinates and relates error to the trailing spectrum.
Replaces raw L2 distance with distance after projection for local functional regression.
Restricts Bayesian optimization to the span of empirical active eigenfunctions rather than random functions.

evaluations.setting: Distributed Poisson control, laminar-jet inverse reconstruction, and kirigami-electronics energy with function-valued controls
evaluations.metric: Estimated spectrum, leading eigenfunctions, and two-dimensional active-coordinate response visualization
evaluations.result: Poisson and laminar examples show most variation in two coordinates; kirigami retains a visible bowl-shaped low-dimensional structure but two coordinates do not capture all variation
evaluations.baseline: No numerical reconstruction-error baseline is reported for the exploratory visualization

evaluations.setting: Leave-one-out KNN regression on each of the three functionals for K from 1 through 20
evaluations.result: The active-projection distance has lower error at the best K on all tasks; on Poisson and kirigami its worst tested K beats the best raw-distance K
evaluations.baseline: KNN using the original Hilbert-space L2 distance

evaluations.setting: Functional Bayesian optimization with 10 initial samples and 40 sequential expected-improvement evaluations, repeated 100 times per task
evaluations.metric: Best observed objective value over evaluations, summarized by median and 10th/90th percentiles
evaluations.result: The active-eigenfunction basis improves faster than the random basis on all three tasks, including rapid recovery after a worse initial projection on the laminar task
evaluations.baseline: A same-size search span formed from randomly sampled input functions

limitations: Author-stated: the method currently treats scalar-valued functionals; vector-valued outputs, multifidelity variants, gradient-free estimation, and mean-gradient modifications are left for future work.

Reviewer-identified: the three application studies are visually and qualitatively summarized in the main text, but exact numerical KNN errors, optimization regret tables, and uncertainty for selected active dimension are not reported there.

Reviewer-identified: all comparisons use one family of active directions and narrow baselines; the paper does not compare against functional PCA, learned neural operators, adaptive bases, or derivative-informed dimension-reduction alternatives on the same tasks.
Reviewer-identified: the empirical operator is defined relative to a user-chosen sampling law, so changing that law can change both the active subspace and downstream conclusions.
Reviewer-identified: operator convergence does not by itself bound discretization error in computed PDE gradients or establish mesh-invariant numerical convergence.
Reviewer-identified: a B-by-B Gram eigendecomposition and B pairwise functional inner products can become costly when gradient sampling is large, even though the ambient dimension is avoided.
Reviewer-identified: isolated simple-eigenvalue convergence does not cover individual eigenfunction interpretation inside clustered or repeated eigenspaces.
Reviewer-identified: the low-dimensional BO experiment uses gradients to construct its search basis and therefore is not directly comparable in total solver cost to a purely black-box optimizer.
failure_modes: A sampling distribution underweights the region containing an optimum, yielding active directions that are predictive locally but exclude the best functional controls.
Nearly tied eigenvalues make individual eigenfunctions unstable across Monte Carlo seeds or mesh refinements.
Noisy adjoints or inconsistent Hilbert inner products cause the Gram matrix to encode discretization artifacts.
A small trailing eigenvalue average hides rare but operationally important directions with large local sensitivity.
The selected active dimension is too small, so projected KNN aliases distinct functions or the BO search basis cannot represent the optimum.
Gradient acquisition dominates the evaluation budget, erasing gains from faster downstream optimization.
A nonlinear low-dimensional manifold exists but cannot be represented well by one global linear active span.
The conditional Poincare-type assumption behind the surrogate error bound fails for the chosen input law.
reusable_insights: Define sensitivity in the native function space before discretization when mesh-independent interpretation matters.
Use a dual Gram eigendecomposition to learn eigenfunctions from sampled gradients without constructing an ambient covariance matrix.
Separate convergence of the statistical operator estimate from convergence of numerical gradients and mesh discretization.
Evaluate a reduced representation by downstream prediction and optimization, not only by an eigenvalue scree plot.
Treat the sampling law as part of the scientific specification because it determines average sensitivity.
Interpret eigenspaces rather than individual eigenfunctions when eigenvalues are repeated or poorly separated.
Charge gradient or adjoint solves to the optimization budget when comparing active-basis search with black-box alternatives.
open_questions: Can the theory jointly control Monte Carlo, PDE discretization, and inexact-adjoint errors in the learned eigenspace?
How should the sampling law adapt during optimization without making the active basis chase transient regions or discard global coverage?
Can nonlinear functional manifolds or operator-valued kernels outperform a single global linear active subspace while retaining interpretable guarantees?
What task-aware criterion should select active dimension when rare-event error matters more than mean-squared error?
How do functional active subspaces compare with derivative-informed projected networks and functional PCA under matched solver budgets?
Can vector-valued outputs and function-valued outputs be handled by one covariance-operator construction with tractable estimation?
How stable are the reported eigenfunctions and BO gains across meshes, input laws, gradient tolerances, and initialization seeds?

competitive_landscape.title: Computing active subspaces with Monte Carlo
competitive_landscape.difference: Constantine and Gleich analyze Monte Carlo recovery of a finite-dimensional active-subspace matrix, including non-asymptotic sampling guidance, bootstrap diagnostics, approximate gradients, and a 100-variable PDE. The reviewed paper transfers the object to a Hilbert-space operator and derives asymptotic operator, eigenfunction, rate, and CLT results, but does not reproduce the prior work's practical bootstrap error analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Large-scale Bayesian optimal experimental design with derivative-informed projected neural network
competitive_landscape.difference: DIPNet uses derivative-informed projections to learn a neural surrogate for PDE parameter-to-observable maps with infinite-dimensional parameter fields and demonstrates experimental-design speedups at discretizations up to 16,641 parameters. The reviewed work instead defines a scalar-functional sensitivity operator in the native Hilbert space and directly reuses its eigenfunctions for analysis and optimization; it offers broader operator theory but no neural surrogate or matched large-scale OED benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: Bayesian functional optimisation with shape prior
competitive_landscape.difference: Vellanki et al. optimize function-valued controls through an adaptive Bernstein-polynomial basis and explicitly incorporate shape priors, without needing target gradients. The reviewed paper chooses a fixed-dimensional basis from sampled functional gradients and shows it can beat random-function spans, providing sensitivity interpretation but requiring gradient access and offering no shape-constraint mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Shared active subspace for multivariate vector-valued functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Musayeva and Binois construct shared active subspaces for multiple finite-dimensional output components by combining gradients or their positive-semidefinite matrices and test several aggregation rules. The reviewed paper handles infinite-dimensional inputs but only scalar outputs, so the two extensions address orthogonal axes and their combination remains future work.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is the first active-subspace analysis defined for real-valued functionals on Hilbert spaces, retaining ridge, surrogate-error, equalization, Monte Carlo consistency, rate, and asymptotic-distribution properties while enabling practical function-space visualization, modeling, and optimization. Reviewer inference: the defensible contribution is the coherent native-Hilbert-space operator formulation plus a dual Gram computation and a set of convergence results tied to functional applications. Finite-dimensional active-subspace Monte Carlo, derivative-informed PDE projections, functional Bayesian optimization, and other infinite-dimensional sensitivity methods all predate it. The main empirical evidence supports usefulness on three curated problems, but does not yet establish numerical mesh invariance, superiority over the strongest derivative-informed or adaptive functional baselines, or end-to-end cost advantage after charging for gradients.

The appendices cited for proofs are not present in this extracted 11-page file, so this reading records theorem statements and stated conditions without independently checking omitted proof details.
